paras: The attempted lynching of James Cunningham took place on a road near Pillow's Bridge, outside Helena, Arkansas, in October 1881, when a disguised mob of about fifty men took three Black prisoners from officers and fired volleys at Cunningham. He was left for dead but was found alive the next morning, and the story of his survival ran in papers from Savannah to Minnesota.

A Globe-Democrat special from Helena reported that James McMath, a young superintendent on Colonel Richardson's plantation at Old Point, fourteen miles below the city, had been shot by unknown parties after a notice warning him to leave was posted. James Cunningham, Henry Lamar and Willie Cunningham were charged with the attempted assassination of J. W. McMath, according to the Helena accounts. Briefer dispatches said the three had been arrested at Oldtown Ridge and charged with the murder of an overseer, whose name appeared as McMath, McGrath or Magrath.

Deputy Sheriff W. B. Lindsey, Constable Cole of Searcy township and special officers Sullivan and Spears were bringing the three men back from Esquire Brand's court by wagon after dark when the mob charged them near Pillow's Bridge. Lindsey drew a pistol and ordered the men to halt, but three of them confronted him with shotguns and told him to keep quiet. The mob led the prisoners from the wagon to a side road and told Jim Cunningham to confess before they shot him; he replied that he was innocent, and several volleys were fired at him.

The mob then handed Lamar and Willie Cunningham back to the officers, who took them to Helena and lodged them in jail. The attackers were disguised and only one or two spoke, so the officers could recognize none of them. The next morning a magistrate summoned a jury and went to the scene to hold an inquest, but the body was gone; after a search, Cunningham was found alive three-quarters of a mile away, having crawled that distance in the dark.

Physicians reported that Cunningham's wound was not dangerous, and he was jailed. He made a statement charging several men with shooting him, and warrants were issued, although the Helena dispatch added that 'all of them can prove an alibi.' According to a Chicago Daily News dispatch, he denied his guilt in the McMath shooting and implicated white men in it, and a posse was in pursuit of the mob. No report of arrests of mob members, or of a trial of either the prisoners or their attackers, appears in the coverage.

The episode reached readers through three channels: the Helena Yeoman's local report, a Helena special to the Little Rock Gazette, and a short Chicago Daily News dispatch. Southern dailies made Cunningham's survival the story, with the Wheeling Intelligencer heading the Gazette special 'Bullet Proof' and the Savannah Morning News calling it 'Twice Riddled'. The Memphis Appeal's headline read 'Can't Kill Him. An Arkansas Negro Who Has Been Twice Shot and Left for Dead Still Alive and Kicking,' and the Memphis Public Ledger called him 'the same darky' who had been left for dead once before.

In the North the Chicago version predominated: the Washington Evening Star printed it as 'Lynch Law in Arkansas' and the Lancaster Intelligencer as 'A Masked Mob'. Midwestern papers such as the St. Paul Globe, the Mower County Transcript and the Watertown Republican reduced it to a line in news or crime roundups through October 26. None of the reports commented on the mob beyond describing it, and the Gazette special's remark that the accused could probably prove an alibi was printed wherever the full text ran.

The Helena Yeoman, as reprinted in the Public Ledger, said the volleys produced 'instant death', while every later report said Cunningham survived. Accounts also differ on the size of the mob, given as fifty in the Helena accounts and forty in a shorter Little Rock version, and on the hour, printed as 8:30, 8:20 or 3 o'clock. Because the Yeoman of the 19th and the Little Rock dispatches of the 20th both say 'last night', the attack may have occurred on October 18 or October 19.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of James Cunningham
bases: A disguised mob of forty to fifty men took three Black prisoners from officers, told one to confess before they shot him, and fired volleys at him, leaving him for dead; he survived (A8, A5, A4).

A mob of forty to fifty acting on an accusation of attempted assassination shot James Cunningham and left him for dead, but he was found alive with a wound physicians called not dangerous (A8, A4, A5); only the Helena Yeoman's first report claimed 'instant death' (A9), so this was an attempted lynching.

Separate Chicago, Little Rock and Helena dispatches agree that a masked mob took the prisoners from officers and shot Cunningham, who survived (A2, A8, A4, A5); the one report of his death (A9) predates the discovery that he was alive.

The Yeoman report was written before the inquest party found Cunningham alive; all later reports say he survived.
